By Erin Handley

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has been asked about artificial intelligence, copyright for Australian artists and whether they will feel let down by the government's approach.

Australian creatives have been clear in saying they want an opt-in process, rather than opt-out, when it comes to their work being used for training AI models.

Opt-out is currently an option on the table.

"The first best option in all of this is for voluntary licensing arrangements to be struck. We've made that very clear," Rowland told ABC Radio National Breakfast.

"And the second point is countries around the world are grappling with this and have different rules.

"We ruled out nearly a year ago now that we would not have a text and data mining exception here in Australia, but we are looking for workable options."

Key Event

By Erin Handley

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has been asked about the rapid review into the OpenAI agent breach of the Medicare statistics portal last week on ABC Radio National Breakfast.

It's unclear if a breach of this kind can be prosecuted under existing law, and Rowland said the taskforce will look at any gaps in legislation.

At this stage, the attorney-general says it's too early to tell if an offence has occurred and if the Australian Federal Police should investigate.

"We need to look at all the evidence first," Rowland says.

"There's a lot of forensics that still needs to be gathered and assessments made on that."

She said while this is a novel technology and the breach itself has been described as "minor" in terms of cybersecurity, "Australians are rightly concerned".

She added that if the tech companies responsible were operating in Australia, the government could regulate them more easily, but it was more complicated when they were located overseas.

"We've had issues of extra-territoriality and certain platforms challenging the jurisdiction of the e-safety commissioner as a regulator, for example — that complicates it more."

By Ewa Staszewska

Senator Larissa Waters has announced she is standing down as Greens leader due to illness, after 16 months in the role.

The Greens have revealed she has been managing an existing kidney disease, which has worsened in recent months.

The 49-year-old notified her colleagues of her decision to step away during a virtual meeting earlier this evening.

Senator Waters expressed gratitude for her stint as leader but admitted she needed to go at a "slower pace" as she focused on her recovery.

"It has been a tremendous honour to be leader of the Greens, fighting for people and the planet," she said in a statement on Monday evening.

"I'm really sad that illness means my time as leader has been cut short, but our movement needs a leader in good health to lead us to success at the next election."

A party room meeting will be held in coming days to discuss the leadership, with ABC told a decision will be made sooner rather than later.

By Joshua Boscaini

The treasurer has finished up his media blitz ahead of the interest rates decision on ABC News Breakfast this morning.

The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to increase interest rates today, which could bring it to 15 year high. It would also be the fourth interest rate hike this year.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers says it is possible to have low unemployment while achieving lower and more steady inflation.
